nodes.title: Art 33 - Powers and functions of the President (single list (a)-(h) as substituted by 20A s.3; no dissolution power here)
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: the earlier title cited 33(2)(c) (summon, prorogue, dissolve Parliament). That was the 19A structure. The current Art 33 (substituted by 20A) is one list (a)-(h); summoning, prorogation and dissolution are now only in Art 70(1). Sampanthan (2018) construed the 19A-era text. 22A (2026) does not touch this provision per parliament.lk summaries (SRC-0039, SRC-0041).

nodes.notes: RESOLVED: Art 35 as substituted by 20A s.5 keeps the proviso allowing Art 126 applications against the AG for the President's official acts; a further proviso excludes the President's power under Art 33(g) (declaring war and peace). nodes.title: Art 107 - Appointment, tenure and removal of judges of SC/CA (retirement ages amended by 22nd Amendment, 2026: SC 67, CA 65; six-year term limit for Chief Justice)
nodes.notes: Arts 107(1)-(4) read in the 2022 text: appointment by President subject to Constitutional Council approval (21A s.12); removal on address by majority of all MPs for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. 107(5) in that text: SC 65, CA 63. 22A (passed and certified 25 Sep 2026) raises these to 67 and 65. The SC determination required a proviso in Clause 2 exempting the sitting Chief Justice from the six-year term limit. 22A also amends Art 137 (Court of Appeal judges 19 to 24). The 22A Act text is not yet read, so this stays corroborated.

nodes.title: Arts 120-124 - Pre-enactment constitutional review of Bills; 14-day petition window (Art 121, 21A); urgent Bills limited to national security and disaster management (Art 122, 20A); bar on other review (Art 124)
nodes.notes: RESOLVED: Art 121(1) window is 14 days from placement on the Order Paper (substituted by 21A s.17); determination within three weeks. Art 122 (inserted by 20A s.26, retained after 21A): Cabinet-certified urgent Bills on national security or disaster management only; SC determination within 24 hours (up to 3 days); not for constitutional amendments. Art 124 bars any other review of Bills. Confirmed in practice by the 22A procedure (SRC-0004). 22A (2026) does not touch this provision per parliament.lk summaries (SRC-0039, SRC-0041).

Liyanage v The Queen
nodes.point: Implied separation of judicial power under the Soulbury Constitution; ad hominem retroactive legislation directed at pending trials usurped judicial power.
nodes.notes: RESOLVED date conflict: delivered 2 Dec 1965 by Lord Pearce; reported 68 NLR 265. Appeals allowed, convictions quashed. Headnote: Part 6 of the Soulbury Constitution shows an intention to keep judicial power in the judicature; an Act usurping it without recourse to s.29(4) is ultra vires. The AC citation was not checked (foreign report).

nodes.name: Bribery Commissioner v Ranasinghe
nodes.point: Bribery Tribunal members appointed otherwise than by the Judicial Service Commission (s.55 Soulbury) invalidly appointed; an Act amending the Constitution without the s.29(4) Speaker's certificate (two-thirds) is invalid - courts must look for the certificate (manner and form).
nodes.notes: Delivered 5 May 1964 by Lord Pearce; appeal dismissed. 'Judicial officers' in s.55 not limited to judges of ordinary courts. The AC citation was not checked.

nodes.name: Ibralebbe v The Queen
nodes.point: Privy Council jurisdiction to entertain criminal appeals from Ceylon survived independence (not abrogated unless the sovereign legislature ends it); the Order in Council implementing a decision is a judicial act.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION of framing: the earlier point ('retention compatible with sovereignty') was loose. The Board held its jurisdiction subsisted and granted special leave; delivered 6 Nov 1963 by Viscount Radcliffe. Reported 65 NLR 433. Note a separate CCA judgment The Queen v Ibralebbe (1963) 65 NLR 472 (joinder of charges) - not this case.

nodes.name: Kodakan Pillai v Mudanayake
nodes.point: Citizenship Act No. 18 of 1948 ss.4-5 and the Parliamentary Elections Amendment Act No. 48 of 1949 are citizenship legislation, not discriminatory legislation contrary to s.29(2)(b) Soulbury Constitution; colourable legislation achieving a forbidden result indirectly would be ultra vires.
nodes.notes: Delivered 11 May 1953 by Lord Oaksey; appeal dismissed.

nodes.name: In re the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution and the Provincial Councils Bill
nodes.point: Neither Bill required a referendum under Art 83 (Sharvananda CJ, Colin-Thome, Atukorale, Tambiah JJ); unitary character unaffected - Provincial Councils are subordinate bodies exercising limited legislative power; devolution without relinquishing supremacy. Ranasinghe J concurred save that proposed Art 154G(2)(b) and (3)(b) required a referendum; Wanasundera, de Alwis, Seneviratne and H. A. G. de Silva JJ dissented (both Bills required a referendum in toto).
nodes.notes: RESOLVED lettering: the judgment text refers to clause 154G(2)(b) and (3)(b) (the headnote OCR drops the G). Hearings 22-30 Oct 1987. Effectively a 5-4 division on the referendum question.

nodes.name: In re the Nineteenth Amendment to the Constitution (2002 Bill)
nodes.point: Organs of government exercise power in trust for the People; transfer, relinquishment or removal of a power attributed to one organ is an alienation of sovereignty inconsistent with Art 3 read with Art 4. Clauses removing the President's dissolution discretion (Art 70) and compelling dissolution on a no-confidence vote required a referendum; clause 6 (conscience vote immune from Art 99(13)) could not be enacted in view of Art 75. Extending the Art 70(1)(a) one-year bar to not more than three years would need only a special majority.
nodes.notes: Hearings 1 and 3 Oct 2002. The 'breadth' dispute (whether every Art 4 inconsistency attracts a referendum) remains an academic question; the Court framed the test as alienation by transfer, relinquishment or removal.

nodes.name: Sampanthan v Attorney General (Dissolution case)
nodes.point: Presidential power of dissolution under Art 33(2)(c) is subject to Art 70; proclamation dissolving Parliament quashed; justiciability of presidential acts via Art 35 proviso.
nodes.notes: Construed the 19A text: Art 33(2)(c) and the Art 70(1)(a) bar of four and a half years. After 20A (2020) Art 33 has no dissolution power and the Art 70 bar is two and a half years (CP-ART-033, CP-ART-070, verified 19 Nov 2026), so the case's holding is tied to repealed wording. Judgment text not yet read: supremecourt.lk is behind a Cloudflare bot challenge.

nodes.name: Mallikarachchi v Shiva Pasupati, Attorney General
nodes.point: Under the original Art 35(1) the President was absolutely immune from proceedings in any capacity; the immunity is personal. Only Art 35(3) matters (functions under Art 44(2)) may be brought against the Attorney-General; an FR challenge to a presidential proscription order (JVP) could not be brought against the AG and failed in limine.
nodes.notes: Decided 11 Feb 1985 (hearings Nov 1984); leave to proceed refused. Pre-19A position; contrast current Art 35(1) proviso (CP-ART-035).

nodes.name: Karunathilaka v Dayananda Dissanayake, Commissioner of Elections
nodes.citation: [1999] 1 Sri LR 157 (SC App 509/98); enforcement order [1999] 1 Sri LR 183
nodes.point: Postponement of provincial council elections violated Art 12(1)/14(1)(a); Art 35 immunity is personal and does not shield the act of others.
nodes.notes: Main judgment 27 Jan 1999 ([1999] 1 Sri LR 157): proclamation and emergency regulation cancelling the poll were executive action; Art 35 does not oust Art 126 over acts of others relying on presidential acts; ouster in s.8 PSO no bar; regulation not for a s.5 PSO purpose; Arts 12(1) and 14(1)(a) infringed (voting is expression). Enforcement judgment 16 Mar 1999 ([1999] 1 Sri LR 183): Commissioner to fix a poll date not later than 27 Apr 1999.

nodes.name: Premachandra v Major Montague Jayawickrema (Provincial Governors' case)
nodes.point: There are no absolute or unfettered discretions in public law; powers are held in trust for the public; Governors' discretion in appointing Chief Ministers is reviewable.
nodes.notes: Order of the Court delivered 16 Aug 1993 (reported 1994). The Art 126(3) reference was held improper; only the Art 125 questions were answered. Answers: Art 154F(4) discretion not purely subjective, justiciable, reviewable by the CA for unreasonableness, bad faith, irrelevant considerations or no evidence.

nodes.name: Gamini Dissanayake v Kaleel
nodes.point: Art 99(13)(a) review of expulsion of eight UNP MPs who signed the 1991 impeachment notice: the Working Committee validly held delegated disciplinary power; the party has primacy over the individual MP and dissent had to be raised internally first. Majority (Fernando J dissenting) held all expulsions valid and found no breach of natural justice, since the Supreme Court hearing was in substance the antecedent hearing; Fernando J upheld only the expulsions of the two Cabinet ministers (SC 5/91, 8/91).
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: the earlier point implied a natural-justice finding in the MPs' favour; the majority upheld the expulsions. Fernando J: party rules are the basis of the exercise of Art 14(1)(c) freedom of association; signing an impeachment notice is a proceeding in Parliament. Hearings 31 Oct-13 Nov 1991; decision date not captured from the headnote.

nodes.name: Velmurugu v Attorney General
nodes.point: Art 11 torture claim: civil standard but a high degree of probability proportionate to the gravity of the allegation; only executive acts are reviewable under Art 126; scope of State liability for subordinate officers (Wanasundera J: administrative practice). Majority held torture not proved and the acts not attributable to the State; application dismissed.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: dissent was by Sharvananda J AND Ratwatte J (record named only Sharvananda J). The dissent would have awarded Rs 10,000 compensation. Decided 9 Nov 1981.

nodes.name: Sriyani Silva v Iddamalgoda, OIC Paiyagala Police
nodes.citation: SC (FR) 471/2000: [2003] 1 Sri LR 14 (preliminary objections, 10 Dec 2002) and [2003] 2 Sri LR 63 (merits, 8 Aug 2003)
nodes.point: Death in police custody: implied right to life read from Arts 11/13(4); heirs/dependants may invoke Art 126 by purposive construction of Art 126(2).
nodes.notes: RESOLVED citation conflict: there are TWO reported judgments in SC 471/2000, not two variant citations. (1) [2003] 1 Sri LR 14, decided 10 Dec 2002 (S. N. Silva CJ, Bandaranayake J, Edussuriya J dissenting): preliminary objections overruled - the deceased acquired a right to redress; where death is causally linked to the infringement anyone with a legitimate interest (here the widow) may prosecute it under Art 126(2); the original petition was in time; Somawathie v Weerasinghe distinguished. (2) [2003] 2 Sri LR 63, decided 8 Aug 2003 (Fernando J): Arts 11 and 13(4) imply a right to life; Art 126(2) read broadly with Art 4(d); Art 17 is an independent fundamental right; Arts 11, 13(2), 17 infringed. Rs 800,000 compensation and costs to the widow and minor child (Rs 700,000 from the State, Rs 50,000 each from the 1st and 2nd respondents personally).

nodes.name: Saman v Leeladasa
nodes.point: Assault of a remand prisoner by a prison guard was executive or administrative action: the test is whether the act was done in the performance (or purported performance) of official duties, not the officer's rank; ostensible-authority acts incidental to employment count even if prohibited. Superior officials are not vicariously liable for subordinates' delicts. The State held liable for Rs 15,000 compensation under Art 11. One-month limit ran only from release from hospital (lex non cogit ad impossibilia).
nodes.notes: RESOLVED (earlier note asked to confirm officer vs State liability): Amerasinghe J (Ranasinghe CJ agreeing) - State liable to pay Rs 15,000; Fernando J - 1st respondent and State jointly and severally liable. Decided 12 Dec 1988; reported [1989] 1 Sri LR 1.

nodes.name: Channa Pieris v Attorney General (Ratawesi Peramuna case)
nodes.point: Arrests under Emergency Regulation 18 read with Reg 23(a) violated Art 13(1): the arresting officer must indicate the procedure under which the arrest is made, detention must be in an authorised place (Reg 19(2)), and there was no basis for reasonable suspicion of an attempt to overthrow the government by unlawful means. Vehement or caustic criticism of the government and calls to 'topple' it by democratic means are not per se unlawful.
nodes.notes: Judgment of Amerasinghe J, 17 June 1994 (hearing 17 Feb 1994). Arts 12, 14(1)(g) and (h) claims not established.

nodes.name: Wickremabandu v Herath
nodes.point: Emergency regulations restricting Arts 13(1)-(2) within Art 15(7) do not override the Constitution; restrictions clearly unreasonable fall outside Art 15(7), but the test is not wholly objective and the court will not usurp the authorities' discretion; preventive detention for national security or public order is not per se unreasonable in a grave emergency, though its abuse remains reviewable.
nodes.notes: Decided 6 Apr 1990 (cited in Dissanayake v Kaleel as 'Wickremabahu v Herath SC 27/1988, SCM 6.4.1990' - the petitioner's name is spelt variously; keep record name per the law report heading).

nodes.name: Joseph Perera v Attorney General
nodes.point: Emergency Regulation 28 (police permission to distribute posters, handbills or leaflets) was a prior restraint with no rational or proximate nexus to national security or public order, so it violated Arts 14(1)(a) and 12 and was invalid; unguided executive pre-censorship is unconstitutional. Majority (Sharvananda CJ and Atukorale J dissenting on this point) held the arrests lawful - the test is the officer's knowledge and state of mind at the time - and detention unlawful only from 15.7.1986. Rs 10,000 compensation payable by the State.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: the earlier point said Reg 28 was 'ultra vires the PSO' and that the 'arrests were illegal'. The text holds Reg 28 invalid for violating Arts 14(1)(a) and 12, and the majority held the arrests lawful. Decided 25 May 1987; reported [1992] 1 Sri LR 199.

nodes.name: Visuvalingam v Liyanage
nodes.citation: [1984] 2 Sri LR 123 (S.C. Applications Nos. 85/83 and 6/84, decided 14 June 1984)
nodes.point: Freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of the recipient, so readers and contributors of the 'Saturday Review' had standing under Art 126 (Rodrigo J dissenting); the recipient's right is subject to Art 15(7); s.8 PSO ouster does not bar relief. Unanimously, the Competent Authority's ban was within the bounds of reasonableness in the emergency, so the applications were dismissed.
nodes.notes: RESOLVED citation conflict: there are FOUR reported SC judgments titled Visuvalingam v Liyanage: (No. 1) [1983] 1 Sri LR 203/236 - nine judges, decided 20 Oct 1983, on the Sixth Amendment oath and Art 157A(7) time limits; [1983] 2 Sri LR 311 - SC 47/83, 53/83, 61/83, decided 18 Nov 1983, closure of the press and company standing (applications dismissed); [1984] 1 Sri LR 305 - SC 74/83, decided 27 Feb 1984, sealing of the newspaper office (leave refused); and [1984] 2 Sri LR 123 - the readers' and contributors' case this record is about. The record id keeps '1983' for stability. Within the 1983 vol 1 report the case begins before p.236; the 19A determination cites it as (1983) 1 Sri LR 236.

nodes.name: Fernando v Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation
nodes.point: Stoppage of the SLBC Non-Formal Education Programme infringed the petitioner's Art 14(1)(a) freedom of speech as a participatory listener; Art 14(1)(a) is not read narrowly - it covers every form of expression, may be invoked with other guarantees (e.g. equality) and includes implied guarantees needed to make it meaningful (e.g. obtaining and recording information). Semble per Fernando J: doubtful that it includes a right to information simpliciter. Relief granted.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: the earlier point ('freedom of speech does not include a free-standing right to information') overstated an obiter doubt (semble) as the holding; the petitioner succeeded. Fernando J also treated earlier right-to-receive dicta (Joseph Perera, Visuvalingam) as obiter in part. Decided 30 Jan 1996.

nodes.name: Faiz v Attorney General
nodes.point: Arrest and detention without compliance with s.109 CCP violated Arts 13(1) and 13(2); assault of the petitioner inside a police station by private persons (5th-7th respondents), made possible by police inaction, was 'executive or administrative action' (Art 11), and failure to act against them denied equal protection (Art 12(1)). Responsibility under Art 126 extends to non-executive respondents guilty of impropriety or connivance with the executive. Per Fernando J: a private act is executive action if done with the executive's authority, express or implied from approval, instigation, connivance, acquiescence, participation or inaction where there is a duty to act, or from later ratification.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION OF A PHASE 2 DOWNGRADE: the 'State authority, connivance or acquiescence' proposition is CONFIRMED from the text (headnote holdings 5-7 and per Fernando J). Goonewardene J dissented on the Art 13(2) detention point. Decided 19 Nov 1993; total Rs 50,000 compensation and Rs 5,000 costs, apportioned among respondents.

nodes.name: Ariyapala Gunaratne v People's Bank
nodes.point: Freedom of association (s.18(1)(f), 1972 Constitution) means primarily the freedom to form and join trade unions; a condition requiring an employee to resign union membership to qualify for promotion was inconsistent with it and could not be imposed by contract; the People's Bank, performing public functions, was 'the State' for this purpose. Restrictions only by law on the s.18(2) grounds.
nodes.notes: MAJOR CORRECTION: the earlier point ('freedom of association includes freedom not to associate', Art 14(1)(d)) is NOT what the case decides. It is a declaratory action under the 1972 Constitution protecting the POSITIVE freedom to join a union. Decided 4 Apr 1986 (Wanasundera J; all agreeing); appeal allowed. Doctrine links to a 'negative freedom of association' need a different authority.

nodes.name: Somawathie v Weerasinghe
nodes.point: Under Art 126(2) a petitioner may complain only of the infringement of his or her own fundamental rights (in person or by an attorney-at-law); a wife had no standing to complain of the infringement of her detained husband's rights. Literal construction (per Amerasinghe J).
nodes.notes: Kulatunga J dissented on the question of law. Decided 20 Nov 1990; application dismissed. Distinguished in Sriyani Silva [2003] 1 Sri LR 14 (death caused by the infringement).

nodes.name: Wickrematunga v Ratwatte
nodes.point: Termination of a petroleum dealership by the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation without cause violated Art 12(1): a contractual power to terminate without reasons does not permit termination at whim; a public corporation must act in good faith and reasonably (no unfettered discretion); the CPC, given State control and functions, is an instrumentality of government bound by Art 12 even in the sphere of contract, and a contractual remedy does not exclude Art 126.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: the earlier point mentioned 'political considerations', which the headnote does not support; the case concerns arbitrariness and Art 12 in State contracts. Decided 17 Dec 1997; reported [1998] 1 Sri LR 201.

nodes.name: Senarath v Chandrika Kumaratunga
nodes.point: Benefits secured by an outgoing President for herself (land, funds, staff) beyond the Presidents' Entitlements Act No. 4 of 1986 violated equality before the law: organs of government are custodians of power and of public property for the People; there is a positive component in the right to equality; public-interest standing to challenge such abuse; the Act, as an exception to equality, is construed strictly. Application allowed; the former President ordered to pay Rs 100,000 costs personally.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: the earlier point referred to 'the limits of presidential immunity after leaving office'; immunity is not discussed in the reported judgment. Personal liability is limited to costs. Decided 3 May 2007 (S. N. Silva CJ).

nodes.name: Transparency International Sri Lanka v Rambukwella (immunoglobulin procurement case)
nodes.citation: SC FR (number to confirm), decided March 2026
nodes.point: Reported: former Health Minister and officials personally liable (Rs. 275 Mn) for Art 12(1) violation in procurement.

nodes.name: Seagull Property Developers FR case
nodes.citation: SC FR (number to confirm), decided 30 Mar 2026
nodes.point: Reported (single commentary) as extending Art 126 relief to private developers - characterisation unverified.

nodes.name: Bulankulama v Secretary, Ministry of Industrial Development (Eppawela case)
nodes.point: Imminent infringement of FR by a proposed phosphate mining agreement at Eppawela; the State's disposal of natural resources must respect environmental law and sustainable development (balancing the needs of present and future generations); Stockholm principles and Rio Principle 15 (precautionary approach) used as guides; public trust doctrine discussed. Under Art 126(4) the respondents were directed to desist from entering into any contract on the deposit until a comprehensive exploration and study was done.
nodes.notes: Decided 2 June 2000 (Amerasinghe J). The phrase 'intergenerational equity' does not appear; the judgment speaks of future generations. Report OCR is letter-spaced; searches run on normalised text.

nodes.name: Bandara v Premachandra, Secretary, Ministry of Lands, Irrigation and Mahaweli Development
nodes.point: Termination of probationer survey trainees by the Surveyor-General on account of trade-union activity (work-to-rule, sick notes) violated Art 12; misconduct had to be dealt with under the Establishments Code. Relief ordered.
nodes.notes: MAJOR CORRECTION: the record cited this case as 'an early articulation of the public trust doctrine'. The reported judgment ([1994] 1 Sri LR 301) contains no public-trust reasoning. It is an Art 12 / trade-union termination case. Its links as key authority for the public-trust doctrines (T-CON-03-04, T-ADM-01-03, S-ADM-01) have been removed. Decided 16 Aug 1993.

nodes.name: Sugathapala Mendis v Chandrika Kumaratunga (Waters Edge case)
nodes.point: Alienation of State land (Waters Edge) for private benefit violated Art 12(1): land and economic assets are administered under the stringent trusteeship of the Public Trust Doctrine for the benefit of all citizens; public-interest standing under Arts 17, 12 and 126; the time limit ran from when the project's nature became manifest; the President cannot shield officials acting against the Constitution or public trust (per Tilakawardane J).
nodes.notes: Judgment of Tilakawardane J (S. N. Silva CJ and Ratnayake J agreeing); relief granted, declarations and orders issued. Hearing 29 May 2008; decision date not captured.

nodes.name: Vasudeva Nanayakkara v Choksy (John Keells / Lanka Marine Services case)
nodes.point: Sale of 90% of shares in Lanka Marine Services Ltd to John Keells Holdings by the PERC Chairman without lawful authority, without a Government Valuer's valuation and in a biased, non-transparent process violated Art 12(1); public-interest standing; under Art 126 the Court may assess severability of the executive action and grant just and equitable relief rather than automatic restoration of the status quo ante.
nodes.notes: RESOLVED page: [2008] 1 Sri LR 134. Decided 21 July 2008. The judgment uses custodianship language for public property; the phrase 'public trust' does not appear in the report.

nodes.name: Environmental Foundation Ltd v Urban Development Authority (Galle Face Green case)
nodes.point: Right of access to information is implicit in Art 14(1)(a) where the matter should be in the public domain and the public interest outweighs confidentiality (pre-Art 14A); the UDA as an organ of government must secure and advance FR under Art 4(d); a bare denial of official information infringed Art 14(1)(a), and the arbitrary refusal infringed Art 12(1). Application allowed; Rs 50,000 costs.
nodes.notes: CORRECTION: decided 23 Nov 2005 (reported 2009). The earlier point attributed 'public trust' to this case; the reported text does not mention it.

nodes.name: Heather Therese Mundy v Central Environmental Authority (Southern Expressway case)
nodes.point: Natural justice owed to affected landowners when route altered post-EIA; compensation; procedural fairness in development decisions.

nodes.name: Nallaratnam Singarasa v Attorney General
nodes.point: Dualism: ICCPR binding internationally but not domestically enforceable without legislation; accession to ICCPR-OP1 by President unconstitutional.

nodes.name: Mudanayake v Sivagnanasunderam
nodes.point: s.3(1)(a) Parliamentary Elections Amendment Act 1949 read with the Citizenship Act 1948 not discriminatory against the Indian community under s.29 Soulbury; clear words make practical effect and motive irrelevant; certiorari lies for error of law on the face.
nodes.notes: Decided 28 Sep 1951; applications allowed (Revising Officer's order quashed). Kodakan Pillai was the 2nd respondent; the PC affirmed in 1953.

nodes.name: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation
nodes.point: Unreasonableness so great that no reasonable authority could have come to it.

nodes.name: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ)
nodes.point: Grounds of review: illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety (proportionality anticipated); legitimate expectation.

nodes.name: Ridge v Baldwin
nodes.point: Revival of natural justice in administrative decisions affecting rights.

nodes.name: Anisminic Ltd v Foreign Compensation Commission
nodes.point: Errors of law go to jurisdiction; ouster clauses do not protect nullities.

nodes.name: Padfield v Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food
nodes.point: Discretion must be used to promote the policy and objects of the statute.

nodes.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
nodes.point: Basic structure doctrine - comparative point for Sri Lankan debates on implied limits to amendment.

nodes.name: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
nodes.point: Procedure established by law must be fair, just and reasonable; interrelation of rights.

Legal System, Sources and Method
nodes.description: The architecture within which every other discipline operates: the plural sources of Sri Lankan law, the court hierarchy and doctrine of precedent, and the techniques of statutory and constitutional interpretation. Not in the original scope list; added because Public Law cannot be learned coherently without it.

nodes.name: Sources of Sri Lankan Law and Legal Pluralism
nodes.tier_basis: Foundational to every discipline; determines which rule applies to a dispute at all.

profile.meaning: The layered sources of law: the Constitution; Acts and subordinate legislation; Roman-Dutch law as the residuary common law; English law received by statute (e.g. commercial matters) and by judicial borrowing; personal/customary laws (Kandyan, Thesawalamai, Muslim law); judicial precedent; and, through incorporation, international law.
profile.significance: Choice-of-law questions (which personal law, whether Roman-Dutch or English law governs) are outcome-determinative and recur in property, family, contract and delict litigation.
profile.history: Dutch administration of the maritime provinces (1658-1796) left Roman-Dutch law; British rule (1796/1815-1948) preserved it while introducing English law in commerce, procedure and evidence, and codifying Kandyan, Tamil (Thesawalamai) and Muslim customs.
profile.foundations: Continuance of existing law (Art 168, Art 16); Civil Law Ordinance 1852; personal-law statutes.
profile.practice: Every pleading implicitly asserts a governing law; personal-law applicability is pleaded and proved.

open_questions: Scope of English law reception under the Civil Law Ordinance in modern commercial disputes.
Constitutional status of personal laws inconsistent with Art 12 (shielded by Art 16).

nodes.name: Roman-Dutch law as residuary common law
nodes.summary: Where no statute or personal law applies, Roman-Dutch law governs private-law questions.

nodes.name: Reception of English law
nodes.summary: Statutory reception in maritime/commercial matters and judicial reception in procedure, evidence and public law.

nodes.name: Personal and territorial laws (Kandyan law, Thesawalamai, Muslim law)
nodes.summary: Law applicable by reason of personal status, religion or domicile/inhabitancy.

related.note: Art 16 preserves existing personal laws from Chapter III challenge

nodes.name: Saving of existing law (Art 16 / Art 168)
nodes.summary: Pre-1978 written and unwritten law remains valid even if inconsistent with fundamental rights.

nodes.name: Court Structure, Jurisdiction and Precedent
nodes.tier_basis: Determines forum, remedy and the binding force of every authority in the database.

profile.meaning: Hierarchy: Supreme Court (final appellate; constitutional, FR, consultative jurisdictions); Court of Appeal (appellate, revision, writs, habeas corpus); High Courts (incl. Provincial High Courts, Commercial High Court, Civil Appellate High Courts); District Courts; Magistrates' Courts; Primary Courts; tribunals.
profile.significance: Writ vs FR forum choice, appeal routes and stare decisis turn on this structure.
profile.history: Charter of Justice 1833; Privy Council appeals abolished by the Court of Appeal (Special Provisions)/1971 legislation (verify); Court of Appeal created by the 1978 Constitution; Provincial High Courts by 13A (1987).
profile.foundations: Chapters XV-XVII and Art 154P of the Constitution; Judicature Act No. 2 of 1978.
profile.practice: Supreme Court decisions bind all lower courts; benches of larger number bind smaller; Privy Council decisions on Ceylon law remain highly persuasive.

open_questions: Exact rules on SC bench size and horizontal precedent (when a fuller bench is constituted).
Effect of the 22nd Amendment (2026) on judicial independence and case backlog - contested.

nodes.name: Stare decisis in Sri Lanka
nodes.summary: Vertical and horizontal precedent; status of Privy Council and pre-1972 decisions.

nodes.name: Jurisdictional allocation between SC, CA and Provincial High Courts
nodes.summary: FR exclusively in SC (Art 126); writs in CA (Art 140) and PHC (Art 154P(4)); overlaps and forum choice.

nodes.name: Statutory and Constitutional Interpretation
nodes.tier_basis: Every legislative and constitutional question is ultimately an interpretive question.

profile.meaning: Rules and presumptions for reading statutes (literal, purposive, mischief; presumptions against retrospectivity, ouster of jurisdiction, and in favour of liberty) and the special canons for the Constitution (generous/purposive construction of rights; reading the Constitution as a whole).
profile.significance: Sri Lanka has no post-enactment review, so interpretation (reading down, presumption of constitutionality) is the main tool for reconciling statutes with rights.
profile.history: Interpretation Ordinance 1901; English canons; post-1978 purposive approach to Chapter III.
profile.foundations: Interpretation Ordinance; Art 125 (SC exclusive interpretation); trilingual texts (Art 23 - Sinhala text prevails in case of inconsistency, verify).
profile.practice: Arguments on Art 126 standing, time limits and 'executive or administrative action' are interpretive battles.

open_questions: Use of unincorporated treaties as aids to interpretation after Singarasa.

nodes.name: Purposive interpretation of fundamental rights
nodes.summary: Rights provisions read generously; e.g. implied right to life and heirs' standing.

nodes.name: Presumption against ouster of jurisdiction
nodes.summary: Courts read finality and ouster clauses narrowly.

nodes.name: Use of international law in interpretation
nodes.summary: Unincorporated obligations as interpretive aids; contested after Singarasa.

nodes.name: Constitutional Law
nodes.description: The 1978 Second Republican Constitution (as amended through the 22nd Amendment, 2026), its history, structure of state power, fundamental rights, devolution, and the institutions that hold power to account.

nodes.name: Constitutional History and Development
nodes.tier_basis: Sri Lankan constitutional doctrine is explicable only through its sequence of constitutions and amendments; frequently relied on in judgments.

profile.meaning: Colebrooke-Cameron reforms (1833) -> Donoughmore Constitution (1931, universal franchise) -> Soulbury Constitution (1946/47; Independence 1948) -> First Republican Constitution (1972, autochthonous, parliamentary supremacy, no judicial review of Acts) -> Second Republican Constitution (1978, executive presidency) -> 22 amendments to date.
profile.significance: Explains the oscillation of executive power (18A/20A expanding; 17A/19A/21A restraining), the absence of post-enactment review, and the unitary-state/devolution tension.
profile.history: Key break-points: Liyanage (1965) on implied separation of powers; 1972 rupture of legal continuity; 1978 presidentialism; 1987 Indo-Lanka Accord and 13A; 2015 19A reforms; 2022 Aragalaya and 21A; 2026 22A on judicial retirement age; promised new constitution not yet begun (Nov 2026).
profile.practice: Historical provisions (e.g. Soulbury s.29) remain relevant to precedent and to the interpretation of continuity provisions.

open_questions: Whether and how the NPP government's promised new constitution will proceed (no drafting process visible as of Nov 2026 - SRC-0013).

nodes.name: Soulbury Constitution and minority protection (s.29)
nodes.summary: Entrenched non-discrimination clause; its limited judicial enforcement.

nodes.name: Autochthony and the 1972 break in legal continuity
nodes.summary: The 1972 Constitution adopted outside the Soulbury amendment procedure to sever colonial legal roots.

nodes.name: The executive presidency (1978) and its amendment cycles
nodes.summary: Pendulum of 17A/18A/19A/20A/21A over presidential power and independent institutions.

nodes.name: Sovereignty, Constitutional Supremacy and Constitutional Amendment
nodes.tier_basis: Defines the legal limits on Parliament and the method of constitutional change; underpins all constitutional review.

profile.meaning: Sovereignty resides in the People (Art 3) and is exercised through organs of government (Art 4). The Constitution is supreme, but judicial control of legislation is only pre-enactment (Arts 120-124); once certified, an Act cannot be questioned (Art 80(3)). Amendment requires a 2/3 majority (Art 82), plus a referendum for entrenched provisions (Art 83).
profile.significance: Sri Lanka is a hybrid: textual supremacy without post-enactment review. Bill challenges are the central constitutional litigation.
profile.history: 1972 Constitution gave Constitutional Court limited pre-enactment review; 1978 transferred this to SC. Doctrine on Arts 3/4 developed in Re 13A (1987) and Re 19A (2002).
profile.practice: Any citizen may petition the SC within a short window after a Bill is placed on the Order Paper; SC determination states majority required (simple, 2/3, or 2/3 plus referendum) and amendments that would cure inconsistency.

open_questions: Is there any implied 'basic structure' limit to amendment in Sri Lanka beyond Art 83? (Comparative: Kesavananda.)
Current statutory window for Art 121 petitions and availability of urgent Bills (Art 122) after 19A/20A/21A - requires verification.

nodes.name: Sovereignty of the People (Arts 3 and 4)
nodes.summary: Powers of government, fundamental rights and franchise as components of inalienable sovereignty.

nodes.name: Balance of power test (Re 19A)
nodes.summary: Transfer/relinquishment of a power of one organ to another, or removal of a check, may infringe Art 3 and require a referendum.

nodes.name: Pre-enactment constitutional review of Bills
nodes.summary: Arts 120-123: SC determines constitutionality of Bills before enactment.

nodes.name: Bar on post-enactment review (Art 80(3) / Art 124)
nodes.summary: Certified Acts are immune from judicial challenge; contrasts with administrative review of subordinate legislation.

related.note: Ultra vires review applies to delegated legislation but not to Acts - tension to investigate

nodes.name: Entrenched provisions and the referendum (Art 83)
nodes.summary: Arts 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and term-extension provisions require a referendum to amend (list to verify against current text).

nodes.name: Unitary State (Art 2) and its meaning
nodes.summary: Whether devolution is compatible with unitary character.

nodes.name: Separation of Powers and Executive Power
nodes.tier_basis: Central to the Sri Lankan constitutional crises (2018 dissolution; 2022) and to the reviewability of presidential acts.

profile.meaning: Distribution of legislative, executive and judicial power (Art 4); the executive President as Head of State, Government and Commander-in-Chief; the Cabinet; presidential immunity (Art 35) and its limits.
profile.significance: Determines whether presidential acts are justiciable and how far the executive can act without Parliament.
profile.history: Liyanage (1965) implied separation of judicial power; 1978 concentrated power in the President; 19A introduced FR review of presidential acts via the AG; 20A re-expanded presidential power; 21A partly reversed it.
profile.foundations: Arts 4, 30-53, 70; public trust conception of power.
profile.practice: Challenges to presidential acts proceed as FR applications against the Attorney-General (Art 35 proviso, as amended - verify current text).

open_questions: Exact scope of the Art 35 proviso after 20A and 21A.
Justiciability of Cabinet policy decisions vs. their implementation.

nodes.name: Separation of judicial power
nodes.summary: Legislature and executive cannot usurp judicial power; ad hominem legislation directed at pending cases is invalid (Soulbury era).

nodes.name: Presidential immunity and its limits
nodes.summary: From absolute immunity (Mallikarachchi) to personal immunity not shielding others' acts (Karunathilaka) to FR review via AG (19A).

related.note: Rule of law limits even the highest executive

nodes.name: Dissolution and prorogation of Parliament
nodes.summary: Art 33(2)(c) read subject to Art 70.

nodes.name: No unfettered discretion / public trust in executive power
nodes.summary: All public power is held in trust for the People and is reviewable.

nodes.name: Cabinet collective responsibility
nodes.summary: Cabinet responsible and answerable to Parliament (Art 42).

nodes.name: Fundamental Rights and Constitutional Remedies
nodes.tier_basis: Most litigated constitutional jurisdiction; Art 12(1) also functions as Sri Lanka's principal vehicle of administrative law review.

profile.meaning: Chapter III rights (Arts 10-14A), restrictions (Art 15), and the Supreme Court's sole and exclusive jurisdiction under Art 126 against infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action, with relief that is just and equitable.
profile.significance: Direct, speedy, apex-court remedy; source of the right-to-life, public trust, legitimate expectation and arbitrariness doctrines in Sri Lanka.
profile.history: 1972 Constitution had rights without effective remedy; 1978 created Art 126; jurisprudence expanded in the 1980s-2000s (state action, standing, compensation); Art 14A added 2015.
profile.foundations: Arts 10-17, 126; Art 16 saving of existing law; Art 15 restrictions; absence of an express right to life.
profile.practice: Petition within one month of the infringement (Art 126(2)); leave to proceed stage; relief includes declarations, compensation (state and personal), directions.

open_questions: Horizontal application to private actors (reported Seagull Property Developers 2026 - verify).
Personal liability of ministers for Art 12 violations (reported Rambukwella 2026 - verify).
Interaction of RTI (Art 14A) with personal data protection.

nodes.name: Art 126 jurisdiction: executive or administrative action
nodes.summary: State action requirement; extended to private conduct with state authority, connivance or acquiescence.

nodes.name: Existing law and Art 16
nodes.summary: Pre-1978 laws inconsistent with Chapter III remain valid; limits FR review of colonial-era statutes and personal laws.

nodes.name: Standing and time limit under Art 126(2)
nodes.summary: Petition by aggrieved person or attorney-at-law; one-month rule and its exceptions; heirs' standing.

nodes.name: Equality and non-discrimination (Art 12)
nodes.summary: Reasonable classification; arbitrariness as inequality; affirmative action (12(4)).

related.note: Arbitrariness doctrine imports administrative-law irrationality into Art 12

nodes.name: Freedom of speech and expression (Art 14(1)(a))
nodes.summary: Includes right to receive information; subject to Art 15(2)/(7) restrictions.

nodes.name: Freedom of assembly and association (Art 14(1)(b)-(d))
nodes.summary: Trade union rights: the freedom to form and join a union cannot be waived by contract or made a condition of promotion (Gunaratne v People's Bank, decided under the 1972 Constitution). Whether Art 14(1)(c)-(d) include a negative freedom not to associate is an open question with no verified Sri Lankan authority yet.

nodes.name: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion (Art 10, 14(1)(e))
nodes.summary: Absolute freedom of thought/conscience (Art 10) vs. restrictable manifestation; interplay with Art 9.

nodes.name: Freedom from torture (Art 11)
nodes.summary: Non-derogable; standard of proof; state and personal compensation.

nodes.name: Personal liberty, arrest and detention (Art 13(1)-(2))
nodes.summary: Arrest according to procedure established by law; reasons; production before judge.

nodes.name: Fair trial, presumption of innocence and non-retroactivity (Art 13(3)-(6))
nodes.summary: Due process guarantees in criminal proceedings; Art 13(6) international-law exception.

nodes.name: Implied right to life
nodes.summary: Derived from Arts 11 and 13(4) though not expressly enumerated.

nodes.name: Right of access to information (Art 14A)
nodes.summary: Constitutional right since 2015, implemented by RTI Act 2016; earlier implied from Art 14(1)(a).

related.note: Art 14A (19A, 2015) constitutionally supersedes the Fernando v SLBC position; this is legislative change, not judicial overruling

nodes.name: Permissible restrictions (Art 15)
nodes.summary: Restrictions 'prescribed by law' for listed purposes; proportionality in Sri Lankan review is underdeveloped.

nodes.name: Remedies: just and equitable relief and compensation
nodes.summary: Declarations, compensation against state and individual officers, directions; personal liability of ministers.

nodes.name: Public interest litigation
nodes.summary: Relaxed standing for issues of public importance (environment, public assets, governance).

nodes.name: The Judiciary and Judicial Independence
nodes.tier_basis: Precondition for every remedy; subject of the latest constitutional amendment (22A, 2026).

profile.meaning: Constitutional protection of judicial power, appointment (President with Constitutional Council approval for superior courts), tenure, removal by address of Parliament (Art 107), the Judicial Service Commission.
profile.significance: The 2012-13 impeachment of Chief Justice Bandaranayake and the 2026 retirement-age amendment illustrate live tensions.
profile.history: Liyanage; 17A/19A/21A appointment controls; impeachment controversy 2012-13 (SC/CA rulings on Standing Order 78A - to be researched); 22A (2026).
profile.practice: Challenges to appointments, transfers and disciplinary control of lower-court judges; contempt jurisdiction.

open_questions: Primary-source research needed: SC Reference on Standing Order 78A (2013) and Court of Appeal writ decision in the Bandaranayake impeachment.
Does extending incumbent judges' tenure (22A) engage judicial independence concerns? (BASL opposed; SC determined 2/3 majority sufficient.)

nodes.name: Security of tenure and removal of superior court judges
nodes.summary: Art 107 address procedure; due-process requirements in removal.

nodes.name: Judicial appointments and the Constitutional Council
nodes.summary: Appointment checks restored by 21A.

nodes.name: Contempt of court
nodes.summary: Constitutional contempt powers of SC/CA and statutory codification (2024 Act - verify).

nodes.name: Parliament, Legislative Power and Parliamentary Privilege
nodes.tier_basis: Important structural subject; litigation frequency lower than FR/writs but central to law-making.

profile.meaning: Parliament's plenary legislative power (Art 75), prohibition on abdication (Art 76), delegated legislation, Standing Orders, privileges and immunities, expulsion of MPs (Art 99(13)).
profile.significance: Frames how laws (and regulations, e.g. under the Online Safety Act or PTA) are made and challenged.
profile.history: Parliament (Powers and Privileges) Act 1953; 1978 proportional representation; party-expulsion litigation in the 1990s.
profile.practice: Delegated legislation reviewed for ultra vires; Bills reviewed pre-enactment.

open_questions: Extent to which Standing Orders and parliamentary procedures are justiciable.

nodes.name: Delegation of legislative power (Art 76)
nodes.summary: Parliament may delegate subordinate rule-making but not abdicate legislative power.

nodes.name: Parliamentary privilege
nodes.summary: Freedom of speech in Parliament; breach of privilege; jurisdiction of SC over offences against Parliament (verify).

nodes.name: Expulsion of MPs from party (Art 99(13))
nodes.summary: SC review of party expulsion; natural justice within parties.

nodes.name: Devolution, the Thirteenth Amendment and Provincial Councils
nodes.tier_basis: High constitutional and political significance; active litigation limited while councils remain unelected (since c. 2017-19).

profile.meaning: Devolution of power to nine Provincial Councils under Chapter XVIIA and the Ninth Schedule (Provincial, Reserved, Concurrent Lists); Governors as presidential appointees; provincial statutes; Provincial High Courts.
profile.significance: Centre-periphery relations, the national question, land and police powers, and the meaning of the unitary State.
profile.history: Indo-Lanka Accord 1987; Re 13A (1987); North-East merger and its de-merger (2006, verify); land and police powers never fully implemented; elections postponed since 2017 amendments; NPP signalling replacement of the PC system in a new constitution (2026).
profile.foundations: Arts 154A-154T; Provincial Councils Act No. 42 of 1987.
profile.practice: Disputes over list allocation, Governors' discretion, provincial statute validity, and election postponement.

open_questions: Legality and remedies for prolonged non-holding of provincial council elections.
Constitutional route to abolish or replace PCs (would it require a referendum?).

nodes.name: Division of legislative competence (Ninth Schedule lists)
nodes.summary: Provincial, Reserved and Concurrent Lists; consultation for concurrent subjects.

nodes.name: Powers and discretion of Governors
nodes.summary: Governors' discretion is reviewable; no unfettered discretion.

nodes.name: Electoral rights and postponement of PC elections
nodes.summary: Franchise as part of sovereignty; executive cannot frustrate elections.

nodes.name: Emergency Powers and National Security
nodes.tier_basis: Recurrent in Sri Lankan history (decades under emergency) and in FR jurisprudence on liberty and expression.

profile.meaning: Proclamation of emergency and emergency regulations under the Public Security Ordinance (Part II) given constitutional force by Art 155; parliamentary approval; overlap with PTA.
profile.significance: Emergency regulations can override ordinary law (but not the Constitution); key site for testing Art 15 restrictions.
profile.history: Near-continuous emergency 1971-2011; 2018 (Kandy), 2019 (Easter attacks), 2022 (Aragalaya) proclamations.
profile.foundations: Art 155; Public Security Ordinance No. 25 of 1947; Art 15(7).
profile.practice: FR challenges to arrests and regulations; review of 'subjective satisfaction'.

open_questions: Reviewability of the proclamation itself (vs. regulations made under it).

nodes.name: Emergency regulations and their constitutional limits
nodes.summary: Regulations cannot override the Constitution; reviewable for consistency with Chapter III.

nodes.name: Preventive detention and subjective satisfaction
nodes.summary: Courts require objective grounds for detention orders.

nodes.name: Constitutional Council and Independent Commissions
nodes.tier_basis: Core of post-2001 accountability architecture; repeatedly amended.

profile.meaning: Constitutional Council's role in approving appointments to superior courts, key offices and independent commissions (Public Service, Police, Elections, Human Rights, Bribery, Audit, Finance, Delimitation, Procurement).
profile.significance: Independence of oversight bodies is the main structural check on the executive presidency.
profile.history: 17A (2001) -> Parliamentary Council (18A, 2010) -> restored (19A, 2015) -> Parliamentary Council (20A, 2020) -> restored (21A, 2022).
profile.practice: Challenges to appointments made without CC approval; commission decisions reviewed by writ or FR.

open_questions: Composition and voting rules of the CC after 21A - verify against current text.

nodes.name: Independence of commissions
nodes.summary: Appointment and removal safeguards; ouster clauses for PSC (Art 61A).

nodes.name: Directive Principles, Constitutional Conventions and Constitutional Morality
nodes.tier_basis: Interpretive and normative rather than directly enforceable; advanced reasoning.

profile.meaning: Non-justiciable Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties (Arts 27-29); constitutional conventions (e.g. caretaker conduct, appointment of PM); constitutional morality as a reasoning device.
profile.significance: Used as interpretive aids (e.g. environment, international law respect in Art 27(15)) and in public-trust reasoning.
profile.history: Borrowed from Irish/Indian models via the 1972 and 1978 Constitutions.
profile.practice: Supporting arguments in FR and writ cases; not stand-alone causes of action.

open_questions: How far courts may use DPSPs to give content to Art 12 or public trust.

nodes.name: Non-justiciability of Directive Principles (Art 29)
nodes.summary: DPSPs guide but do not confer enforceable rights.

nodes.name: Constitutional conventions
nodes.summary: Non-legal rules of political practice; role in 2018 crisis.

nodes.name: Identity Provisions - Language, Religion and Citizenship
nodes.tier_basis: Historically central to ethnic conflict and constitutional reform; entrenched provisions.

profile.meaning: Official and national languages (Chapter IV, Sinhala and Tamil official, English link language); Buddhism's foremost place (Art 9); citizenship and statelessness.
profile.significance: Language rights in administration and courts; religion-state relationship (conversion bills, places of worship); historical citizenship laws.
profile.history: Official Language Act 1956; Tamil official language via 13A/16A; Citizenship Act 1948 and Kodakan Pillai; Grant of Citizenship to Persons of Indian Origin Act 2003 (verify).
profile.practice: Language-rights complaints (Official Languages Commission); Bill challenges on religious matters.

open_questions: SC determinations on anti-conversion/incorporation Bills (e.g. Teaching Sisters of the Holy Cross, c. 2003) - to research and verify.

nodes.name: Language rights
nodes.summary: Right to use Sinhala or Tamil in dealings with the State and courts.

nodes.name: Article 9 and religious freedom
nodes.summary: Foremost place to Buddhism balanced against Arts 10 and 14(1)(e).

nodes.name: Administrative Law
nodes.description: Judicial and non-judicial control of public power. A distinctive Sri Lankan feature is the dual track: writ review in the Court of Appeal (Art 140) and Provincial High Courts (Art 154P(4)), and rights-based review in the Supreme Court through Art 12(1) under Art 126.

nodes.name: Foundations of Judicial Review and the Rule of Law
nodes.tier_basis: Conceptual base for all review; links constitutional structure to administrative remedies.

profile.meaning: Public power exists only within legal limits; courts review legality, not merits. In Sri Lanka, review is grounded in the Constitution (Arts 3, 4, 12, 126, 140) and the received English common law of judicial review.
profile.significance: Defines when a decision can be challenged at all and on what conception of power (public trust).
profile.history: Inherited English prerogative writs (Courts Ordinance / Charter of Justice); constitutionalised in 1978; public trust doctrine developed from the 1990s.
profile.foundations: Rule of law; no unfettered discretion; public trust; sovereignty of the People.
profile.practice: Framing a challenge: public-law character of the decision, forum, grounds, remedy.

open_questions: Is the public trust doctrine a free-standing ground of review or a gloss on Art 12 and ultra vires?

nodes.name: Legality vs merits distinction
nodes.summary: Courts do not substitute their decision for the administrator's.

nodes.name: Rule of law and no unfettered discretion
nodes.summary: Every power has legal limits however widely expressed.

nodes.name: Public trust doctrine
nodes.summary: Public power and resources are held in trust for the People; decisions must serve public purposes.

related.note: Eppawela extended public trust to natural resources

nodes.name: Constitutionalisation of administrative law through Art 12(1)
nodes.summary: Arbitrary, unreasonable or unfair administrative action treated as denial of equality, making Art 126 a review forum.

nodes.name: Writ Jurisdiction and Public-Law Remedies
nodes.tier_basis: Most frequently used review procedure in practice; essential procedural knowledge.

profile.meaning: Certiorari (quash), prohibition (restrain), mandamus (compel performance of a public duty), quo warranto (challenge title to office), procedendo, and habeas corpus (Art 141); issued by the Court of Appeal and, for provincial matters, Provincial High Courts.
profile.significance: Writs are the default remedy for unlawful administrative decisions not engaging fundamental rights or where the one-month FR deadline has passed.
profile.history: English prerogative writs; constitutional basis from 1978 (Art 140); PHC writ jurisdiction from 13A.
profile.foundations: Arts 140, 141, 154P(4); Court of Appeal (Appellate Procedure) Rules (verify citation).
profile.practice: Discretionary remedies: barred by undue delay/laches, availability of alternative remedy, futility, suppression of material facts; necessary parties; amenability (public vs contractual/private functions).

open_questions: Amenability of state-owned companies and contractual decisions to writs - to research with primary authorities.
Phase 2 priority: identify leading CA/SC authorities on delay, alternative remedy and suppression.

nodes.name: Amenability: public law vs private law functions
nodes.summary: Writs lie against bodies exercising public functions; contractual matters generally excluded.

nodes.name: Certiorari and prohibition
nodes.summary: Quashing and restraining orders for decisions affecting rights made in excess/abuse of power.

nodes.name: Mandamus
nodes.summary: Compels performance of a public duty owed to the applicant; no mandamus against the President personally (verify) or for discretionary outcome.

nodes.name: Quo warranto
nodes.summary: Challenges the legal right of a person to hold a public office.

nodes.name: Habeas corpus
nodes.summary: Production of a detained person; enforced disappearances context.

nodes.name: Discretionary bars: delay, alternative remedy, futility, suppression
nodes.summary: Grounds on which relief may be refused despite illegality.

nodes.name: Grounds of Judicial Review
nodes.tier_basis: The substantive content of every review application.

profile.meaning: Illegality (ultra vires, error of law, improper purpose, relevant/irrelevant considerations, fettering, unlawful delegation), irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness), procedural impropriety; proportionality as an emerging ground.
profile.significance: Shared grammar between writ review and Art 12 review.
profile.history: English common law (Wednesbury 1948; GCHQ 1985; Anisminic 1969) received and adapted by Sri Lankan courts.
profile.foundations: Ultra vires principle; statutory purpose; rule of law.
profile.practice: Plead grounds precisely; produce the record and reasons.

open_questions: Has proportionality been adopted as an independent ground by the Sri Lankan Supreme Court? Identify primary authority.

nodes.name: Ultra vires (substantive and procedural)
nodes.summary: Acting outside statutory power or failing mandatory procedure; applies to delegated legislation.

nodes.name: Error of law and jurisdictional error
nodes.summary: Errors of law render decisions void and outside ouster protection.

nodes.name: Irrationality / Wednesbury unreasonableness
nodes.summary: Decision so unreasonable no reasonable authority could reach it.

nodes.name: Relevant and irrelevant considerations; improper purpose; abuse of power
nodes.summary: Discretion exercised for statutory purposes, taking account of relevant matters only.

nodes.name: Fettering and failure to exercise discretion; unlawful delegation; acting under dictation
nodes.summary: Rigid policies, abdication or dictation by superiors vitiate decisions.

nodes.name: Ouster and finality clauses
nodes.summary: Narrow construction; Art 61A (PSC) and statutory finality clauses; constitutional FR jurisdiction preserved.

nodes.name: Proportionality
nodes.summary: Least-restrictive means and fair balance - status in Sri Lanka requires investigation.

nodes.name: Procedural impropriety
nodes.summary: Breach of statutory procedure or natural justice.

nodes.name: Natural Justice and Procedural Fairness
nodes.tier_basis: Arises in nearly every disciplinary, licensing and adjudicative public decision.

profile.meaning: Audi alteram partem (fair hearing: notice, disclosure, opportunity to respond) and nemo judex in causa sua (rule against bias); duty to give reasons as an emerging component.
profile.significance: Most successful ground in public service and disciplinary litigation.
profile.history: Ridge v Baldwin revival; Sri Lankan application to universities, public service, development projects (Southern Expressway).
profile.foundations: Common law presumption that Parliament intends fair procedure; Art 12 equal protection.
profile.practice: Content varies with context; legislative functions traditionally excluded.

open_questions: Is there a general duty to give reasons in Sri Lankan administrative law? Identify SC authority.

nodes.name: Audi alteram partem (right to be heard)
nodes.summary: Notice of case, opportunity to respond, disclosure of adverse material.

nodes.name: Nemo judex in causa sua (rule against bias)
nodes.summary: Actual and apparent bias; pecuniary and personal interest.

nodes.name: Duty to give reasons
nodes.summary: Reasons as element of fairness and enabling review; RTI interplay.

nodes.name: Legitimate Expectation
nodes.tier_basis: Doctrinally important and evolving; links fairness, equality and good administration.

profile.meaning: Protection of expectations induced by public authorities' promises or practices: procedural (right to be consulted/heard) and substantive (to receive the promised benefit).
profile.significance: Frequently pleaded in public service, land, licensing and investment disputes; overlaps with Art 12.
profile.history: Received from English law (GCHQ); developed in Sri Lankan cases in the 1990s-2000s (authorities to be verified in Phase 2).
profile.practice: Clear and unambiguous representation; reliance; overriding public interest.

open_questions: Primary authorities on substantive legitimate expectation in Sri Lanka (candidates from memory require verification before entry).

nodes.name: Procedural legitimate expectation
nodes.summary: Expectation of a hearing or consultation before change.

nodes.name: Substantive legitimate expectation
nodes.summary: Expectation of a substantive benefit; balanced against public interest.

nodes.name: Public Service Law and Disciplinary Proceedings
nodes.tier_basis: High volume of FR and writ litigation (appointments, promotions, transfers, discipline).

profile.meaning: Constitutional regime for appointment, promotion, transfer, discipline and dismissal of public officers (PSC and delegated authorities), Establishments Code, appeals to the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, and Art 61A's ouster with FR preserved.
profile.significance: The largest single category of Art 12(1) applications.
profile.history: Colonial civil service; 1972 Cabinet control; 17A/19A/21A independent PSC.
profile.foundations: Chapter IX; AAT Act No. 4 of 2002; Establishments Code (administrative rules).
profile.practice: Schemes of recruitment and marking schemes; disciplinary inquiries; transfer policies.

open_questions: Legal status of the Establishments Code (rules vs law) - verify.

nodes.name: Appointments and promotions under Art 12(1)
nodes.summary: Adherence to approved schemes; arbitrariness and political victimisation.

nodes.name: Disciplinary inquiries and fair procedure
nodes.summary: Charge sheet, inquiry, opportunity to defend, impartial inquirer.

nodes.name: Government Contracts, Procurement, Licensing and Regulatory Decisions
nodes.tier_basis: Large commercial and governance significance; less settled law.

profile.meaning: Review of state contracting, tender processes, alienation of state land and assets, privatisation, and regulatory licensing decisions.
profile.significance: Corruption prevention; investor protection; public trust over public assets.
profile.history: Public trust cases (Waters Edge, Lanka Marine Services) and procurement litigation; post-2022 governance reforms (Anti-Corruption Act 2023; PFMA 2024).
profile.foundations: Public trust; Art 12; procurement guidelines; National Procurement Commission (verify current status).
profile.practice: Tender challenges by writ or FR; interim relief against award.

open_questions: Legal force of procurement guidelines; current statute on public procurement (a Public Procurement Bill/Act may exist - verify).

nodes.name: Public trust over state assets and land
nodes.summary: State disposal of assets must serve public interest and be transparent.

nodes.name: Review of tender and procurement decisions
nodes.summary: Public-law amenability of procurement despite contractual setting.

nodes.name: Administrative Tribunals, Ombudsman and Commissions of Inquiry
nodes.tier_basis: Specialised mechanisms; important for completeness and accountability.

profile.meaning: Non-court adjudication and oversight: Administrative Appeals Tribunal, Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration, HRCSL inquiries, RTI Commission appeals, Commissions of Inquiry and Presidential Commissions.
profile.significance: Accessible remedies; quasi-judicial bodies subject to review; Presidential Commissions' findings and civic disability.
profile.history: Commissions of Inquiry Act 1948; Special Presidential Commissions of Inquiry Law 1978 (civic disability controversy).
profile.practice: Exhaustion vs. direct review; evidential status of commission findings.

open_questions: Legal effect of Presidential Commission of Inquiry findings on subsequent prosecutions.

nodes.name: Review of tribunals and commissions
nodes.summary: Quasi-judicial bodies bound by natural justice; findings reviewable by writ.

nodes.name: Human Rights and International Law
nodes.description: International law's reception into Sri Lankan law, international human rights obligations and oversight mechanisms, and comparative constitutional jurisprudence. Will later expand into a separate general Public International Law discipline (D-INT, planned).

nodes.name: Reception of International Law (Dualism, Incorporation, Customary Law)
nodes.tier_basis: Determines whether international norms are usable in domestic litigation at all.

profile.meaning: Sri Lanka is treated as dualist for treaties: ratified treaties bind the State internationally but create domestic rights only when incorporated by legislation. Status of customary international law in domestic courts is less settled.
profile.significance: Shapes the use of ICCPR, CAT and other treaties in FR and criminal cases.
profile.history: Singarasa (2006) on ICCPR and OP1; ICCPR Act 2007 as partial incorporation; 2008 advisory opinion on ICCPR compliance (to verify); earlier courts used treaties as interpretive aids (Bulankulama).
profile.foundations: No general constitutional incorporation clause; Art 27(15) DPSP; Art 157 (investment treaties); Art 13(6) refers to general principles of international law.
profile.practice: Argue treaties as interpretive aids; rely on incorporating statutes (CAT Act, ICCPR Act).

open_questions: Status of the 2008 SC advisory opinion (Art 129 reference) on ICCPR rights - locate primary text.
Is customary international law part of the law of Sri Lanka without legislation?

nodes.name: Dualism and treaty incorporation
nodes.summary: Treaties require legislation for domestic effect; treaty-making as executive act.
